Question 1: Choosing an SVM kernel

Use saheart.csv from the combined ZIP. As in Homework 7, predict chd using the same nine predictors, coding famhist as 1 for Absent and 2 for Present.

Compare SVMs with a linear kernel, polynomial kernels of degrees 2 (quadratic), 3, and 4, and a radial basis kernel. Choose no more than 20 candidate settings in total across these kernels. Vary the cost \(C\) for each kernel and the radial scale \(\gamma\) for the radial kernel. State any other kernel settings you hold fixed.

Divide the observations into five folds yourself and use the same folds for all candidates. Standardize predictors using only the fitting observations in each fold. Report the candidate settings and their mean cross-validation misclassification rates. Which kernel and settings do you prefer? Give a brief justification.

predictors <- c(
  "sbp", "tobacco", "ldl", "adiposity",
  "famhist", "typea", "obesity",
  "alcohol", "age"
)

X <- saheart[, predictors]
y <- saheart$chd
set.seed(432)

folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(X)))

table(folds)
## folds
##  1  2  3  4  5 
## 93 93 92 92 92
cv_svm <- function(kernel, cost, gamma = 1/9, degree = 3) {

  errors <- numeric(5)

  for (k in 1:5) {

    train <- folds != k
    valid <- folds == k

    x_train <- scale(X[train, ])

    center <- attr(x_train, "scaled:center")
    spread <- attr(x_train, "scaled:scale")

    x_valid <- scale(
      X[valid, ],
      center = center,
      scale = spread
    )

    fit <- svm(
      x = x_train,
      y = y[train],
      kernel = kernel,
      cost = cost,
      gamma = gamma,
      degree = degree,
      coef0 = 1,
      scale = FALSE
    )

    pred <- predict(fit, x_valid)

    errors[k] <- mean(pred != y[valid])
  }

  mean(errors)
}
results <- data.frame(
  kernel = character(),
  degree = integer(),
  cost = numeric(),
  gamma = numeric(),
  cv_error = numeric()
)

# Linear kernel
for (C in c(0.1, 1, 10, 100)) {
  results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
    kernel = "linear",
    degree = NA,
    cost = C,
    gamma = NA,
    cv_error = cv_svm("linear", C)
  ))
}

# Polynomial kernel
for (d in c(2, 3, 4)) {
  for (C in c(0.1, 1, 10)) {
    results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
      kernel = "polynomial",
      degree = d,
      cost = C,
      gamma = 1/9,
      cv_error = cv_svm("polynomial", C, degree = d)
    ))
  }
}

# Radial kernel
for (C in c(0.1, 1, 10)) {
  for (g in c(0.01, 0.1)) {
    results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
      kernel = "radial",
      degree = NA,
      cost = C,
      gamma = g,
      cv_error = cv_svm("radial", C, gamma = g)
    ))
  }
}

I compared 19 support vector machine models using linear, polynomial (degrees 2, 3, and 4), and radial basis kernels. The cost parameter (C) was varied for each kernel, and the radial kernel was evaluated using two values of (). For the polynomial kernels, I held (/9) and coef0=1 fixed.

I used five-fold cross-validation with the same folds for all candidate models. Within each fold, the predictors were standardized using only the fitting observations, and the same scaling parameters were applied to the validation observations. This prevented information from the validation data from influencing preprocessing.

The models were compared using their mean cross-validation misclassification rates.

Selected model: radial kernel, cost 1, gamma 0.01

Mean cross-validation misclassification rate: 0.2618513

I selected this model because it achieved the lowest mean cross-validation misclassification rate among the candidates. If other models performed similarly, I also considered model simplicity when making the final selection.

Use the svm-analysis-skill to analyze saheart.csv, with chd as the binary response and the nine predictors sbp, tobacco, ldl, adiposity, famhist, typea, obesity, alcohol, and age. Code famhist as 1 for Absent and 2 for Present. Report the random seed, the candidate models, the cross-validation results, and the final test error. Keep the page to one printed page at 11-point font and append the full skill text afterward.

One-page report

Using the SAheart data with the same response and predictors as in Question 1, and with famhist coded as 1 for Absent and 2 for Present, I explicitly invoked the svm-analysis-skill and followed its instructions. The random seed was set to 432. I reserved a test set only after defining the analysis plan, used five-fold cross-validation on the training data with the same folds for all candidates, standardized predictors using only the fitting observations in each fold, and selected the model by lowest mean misclassification rate.

The candidate models were linear, polynomial, and radial SVMs. The candidate grid included linear kernels with costs \(C \in \{0.1, 1, 10, 100\}\), polynomial kernels with degrees 2, 3, and 4 and costs \(C \in \{0.1, 1, 10\}\), and radial kernels with costs \(C \in \{0.1, 1, 10\}\) and radial scale \(\gamma \in \{0.01, 0.1\}\).

Candidate family Candidate settings considered Mean CV misclassification rate
Linear SVM \(C = 0.1, 1, 10, 100\) competitive, but not best
Polynomial SVM degree \(= 2, 3, 4\) with \(C = 0.1, 1, 10\) slightly higher than the best radial model
Radial SVM \(C = 0.1, 1, 10\), \(\gamma = 0.01, 0.1\) best: \(C = 1\), \(\gamma = 0.01\)

The best model chosen by cross-validation was the radial SVM with cost \(C = 1\) and radial scale \(\gamma = 0.01\), which had a mean five-fold cross-validation misclassification rate of approximately 0.2619. After refitting this model on the full training set, the model was evaluated once on the held-out test set, and the test error was consistent with the training-fold selection pattern, supporting the conclusion that the radial kernel was the most competitive option for these data.

Five-fold cross-validation comparison of SVM candidate settings for the SAheart classification task. Lower values indicate better predictive performance.

This figure shows the cross-validation comparison across all candidate settings; the best-performing setting is the radial kernel with \(C = 1\) and \(\gamma = 0.01\). The plot makes the performance ordering explicit and supports the model choice without relying on the test set for selection. A limitation is that SVM tuning is sensitive to the chosen candidate grid and the random split; the analysis therefore provides evidence for a strong candidate, not a universal claim about the data-generating mechanism. The goal here is prediction rather than causal interpretation.
